result.title: Agent._log_next_action_summary() builds a debug log line and then discards it
result.defect: `Agent._log_next_action_summary()` (browser_use/agent/service.py, originally lines 2094-2124, called once per step from `get_model_output()` at line ~1994 via `self._log_next_action_summary(parsed)`) has the docstring "Log a comprehensive summary of the next action(s)". It gates on `self.logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)`, then loops over `parsed.action`, building a formatted `name(params...)` string per action into a local list `action_details` (handling `index`, `text`, `url`, `success`, and other scalar params) — and then the function simply ends. `action_details` is never passed to a logger call, never returned, never used. The function is a pure no-op with respect to its own contract: an operator who turns on DEBUG logging to see what action the agent is about to take gets nothing from this call site. This is distinct from the module-level `log_response()` (also called in `get_model_output`), which logs thinking/eval/memory/next_goal but never the concrete action name or its parameters — so this wasn't redundant with existing logging, it was a genuine, silently-dropped piece of functionality. Compare the sibling method `_log_step_completion_summary` (same file, ~line 2163), which builds a very similar `message` string and explicitly does `self.logger.debug(message); return message` — the missing final call in `_log_next_action_summary` is the anomaly, not the norm, in this file.
result.self_critique: Checked the alternatives before committing to this fix: (1) Is it intentional? No — the entire body exists solely to build `action_details`; an intentional no-op wouldn't gate on `isEnabledFor(DEBUG)` and then do real formatting work for nothing. (2) Is it dead code that should be deleted rather than "fixed"? No — `log_response()` (the other logging call in the same `get_model_output()`) never logs the actual action name/params, only thinking/eval/memory/next_goal, so this fills a real, distinct gap rather than duplicating existing output. (3) Does an existing test cover it? Grepped `tests/ci` for `_log_next_action_summary` and `Next action` — no hits; none of the existing suites (test_budget_warning.py, test_action_loop_detection.py, etc.) touch this method. (4) Would fixing it break public/documented behavior? No — it's a private (`_`-prefixed), `-> None` helper called only internally; adding a `logger.debug(...)` call only affects DEBUG-level log output, not return values, not the action protocol, not any documented API. (5) Verified my own test methodology, which initially gave a false negative: `browser_use/logging_config.py:161` sets `propagate = False` on the `browser_use` logger once `setup_logging()` has run, so pytest's `caplog` (root-attached) cannot see `Agent` logger records regardless of level — my first test draft used caplog and failed identically on both fixed and unfixed code for the wrong reason (a test-harness bug, not the target bug). I diagnosed this by reading `logging_config.py`, rewrote the test to attach a handler directly to `logging.getLogger('browser_use')`, and reran both variants to confirm the test now discriminates correctly (fails only on unfixed code, passes only on fixed code).
result.fix_summary: Added the missing final log call at the end of `Agent._log_next_action_summary()`: `if action_details: self.logger.debug(f'📝 Next action(s): {" | ".join(action_details)}')`. Three-line, minimal, behavior-additive change (only emits a DEBUG-level log line the docstring already promised); no other logic touched.

result.title: evaluate() silently corrupts valid JS containing escaped quotes inside strings
result.defect:
`Tools._validate_and_fix_javascript()` (browser_use/tools/service.py, old lines 2053-2059, now 2053-2072) runs unconditionally on every `evaluate()` call (invoked at line 1954: `validated_code = self._validate_and_fix_javascript(code)`). Its "Pattern 1" step was:
```
# Pattern 1: Fix double-escaped quotes (\\\" → \")
fixed_code = re.sub(r'\\"', '"', code)
```
This regex matches every literal backslash-quote pair (`\"`) anywhere in the submitted JS and strips the backslash entirely, regardless of context. This is meant to repair a specific artifact (a whole script that arrived over-escaped by an upstream JSON layer), but it cannot distinguish that from perfectly valid JS that legitimately escapes a quote *inside* a double-quoted string literal (e.g. `"She said \"hi\""`, a completely ordinary and common JS pattern). For the valid case, stripping the backslash corrupts `"She said \"hello\" to me"` into `"She said "hello" to me"`, an unambiguous JS syntax error. I verified this both at the pure-regex level (`.venv/bin/python3 -c ...`) and end-to-end through a real `BrowserSession` + CDP: `tools.evaluate(code='(function(){ return "She said \\"hello\\" to me"; })()', ...)` returned `ActionResult(error='JavaScript Execution Failed: ... Uncaught ... Validated Code (after quote fixing): (function(){ return "She said "hello" to me"; })()')` instead of succeeding. This directly contradicts the function's own docstring ("Validate and fix common JavaScript issues before execution") — it breaks otherwise-correct code the agent wrote, and the agent has no way to "fix" its own valid code in response to the resulting syntax error, since the corruption happens invisibly after submission. There was zero test coverage for this function (confirmed via grep across tests/ and browser_use/) and all existing `evaluate()`-adjacent tests only exercise raw CDP `Runtime.evaluate`, never the action's fixer.
result.self_critique: Before touching anything I checked for the simpler "this is intentional/tested" explanation that the task explicitly warns against forcing a fix past: I first suspected a bug in the `navigate()` empty-DOM retry logic (the final retry check narrows from `_page_appears_empty()` to just `_root is None`), but tests/ci/test_action_blank_page.py (lines 174-195) explicitly documents and asserts that exact narrower behavior as intentional design ("Error is only returned when _root is None... avoids false positives on image-only or other non-interactive-but-valid pages") — so I dropped that finding rather than force it. For the quote-corruption bug, I considered whether the "over-escaping" the fixer targets might be common enough that this is an acceptable trade-off deliberately made by the author — but the case I broke (a quote escaped *inside* a string, with the string's own delimiter quotes left bare) is objectively common/legitimate JS, not a rare edge case, and there's no comment or test acknowledging this trade-off; it reads as an oversight, not a documented compromise. I also checked whether a heuristic distinguishing the two cases even exists: it does — the over-escaped-artifact case has *zero* unescaped delimiter quotes anywhere in the payload (every quote, including the ones meant to delimit the string, got the extra backslash), while the legitimate-inner-escape case always has bare delimiter quotes. That gave me a principled, minimal, deterministic condition to gate the fix on, rather than just neutering the feature outright — I verified both the "still fixes genuine over-escaping" and "no longer corrupts valid escaped quotes" cases hold after the change. Because `_validate_and_fix_javascript` is a private helper (leading underscore) called only internally by `evaluate()`, narrowing when it fires doesn't change any documented/public API contract — it only stops it from firing in a case it was never supposed to touch.
result.fix_summary: Guarded Pattern 1's backslash-quote stripping behind a check that it only fires when the code contains *no* unescaped (bare) double-quote at all — the unambiguous signature that the whole script got over-escaped by an upstream layer. When the code already has proper bare delimiter quotes around its strings (i.e. it's valid JS that just happens to also escape a quote inside one of those strings), the code is left untouched. This keeps the "fix a fully over-escaped script" behavior working while eliminating the corruption of legitimately-escaped valid JS.

result.title: reset() never clears _closed_popup_messages, so auto-dismissed dialogs resurface forever
result.defect: `BrowserSession._closed_popup_messages` (session.py:707, `PrivateAttr(default_factory=list)`, "Store messages from auto-closed JavaScript dialogs") is appended to by `PopupsWatchdog.handle_dialog` every time it auto-accepts a JS `alert`/`confirm`/`prompt`/`beforeunload` (browser_use/browser/watchdogs/popups_watchdog.py:71), and copied verbatim into every `BrowserStateSummary` by `DOMWatchdog` (browser_use/browser/watchdogs/dom_watchdog.py:356/503/546), which `agent/prompts.py:323-329` renders into the LLM prompt every single step as "Auto-closed JavaScript dialogs". Nothing in the codebase ever clears this list (verified via grep: zero `.clear()` or reassignment sites). `reset()` (session.py:775-838), whose docstring is "Clear all cached CDP sessions with proper cleanup" and which explicitly clears the directly analogous per-session caches `_cached_selector_map`, `_cached_selector_indices` and `_downloaded_files` at lines 810-812, omits `_closed_popup_messages`. Net effect: a dialog closed before a `stop()`/`start()` or `kill()`/`start()` reuse of the same `BrowserSession` object keeps being reported to the LLM as a freshly-closed dialog in every subsequent state for the rest of the object's life, and even within one continuous session the list grows without bound (never trimmed), so a page that pops many dialogs bloats every future prompt with repeated stale text.
result.self_critique: Checked the alternatives before committing to this: (1) intentional design? No — the sibling caches cleared right next to it (`_downloaded_files` etc.) share the identical "per-session, track during this session" comment style, and `closed_popup_messages` in prompts.py is phrased as "auto-closed" (present/recent), not a permanent transcript, so silently replaying old entries forever contradicts the field's own framing; there's no doc or comment anywhere claiming session-spanning accumulation is wanted. (2) existing test coverage? grepped tests/ — only two unrelated tests pass `closed_popup_messages=[]` as a static fixture value; nothing exercises accumulation or clearing. (3) compatibility break? `_closed_popup_messages` is a private attribute (leading underscore, `PrivateAttr`), not public API, so clearing it in `reset()` changes no documented contract. (4) simpler explanation missed? Considered whether PopupsWatchdog itself should drain the list after each state capture instead — that would be the more complete fix, but it lives in `browser_use/browser/watchdogs/dom_watchdog.py`, outside my assigned file; the omission in `reset()` is still a real, independently-fixable bug (state must not survive an explicit session reset) and is the piece owned by `session.py`. I also noticed and set aside two other candidates as weaker: (a) a suspected `AttributeError` in `on_NavigateToUrlEvent` from an unguarded `session_manager.get_target(current_target_id)` — traced through `_handle_target_detached` and found `agent_focus_target_id` is always cleared synchronously and atomically before the target is removed from `_targets`, so the crash isn't actually reachable; (b) a possible race between WS-drop detection and `_reconnecting` flag being set — real in principle but not reliably reproducible without mocking internals, which the test rules for this exercise forbid.
result.fix_summary: Added `self._closed_popup_messages.clear()` to `BrowserSession.reset()` in browser_use/browser/session.py, immediately after the existing `self._downloaded_files.clear()` line, so it is cleared alongside the other per-session caches `reset()` already owns.

result.title: Fix CDP remote-object handle leak in JS click-listener detection
result.defect: In `DomService._get_all_trees` (browser_use/dom/service.py, click-listener detection block, originally lines ~463-567), the JS click-listener scan runs `Runtime.evaluate` (no `objectGroup`) to get an array of elements with click listeners, then `Runtime.getProperties` on that array to pull out each individual element's own remote-object handle (`element_object_ids`), then `DOM.describeNode` per handle to resolve backend node IDs. Afterward the code released only the array's own handle: `Runtime.releaseObject(params={'objectId': result_object_id}, ...)` (old lines 556-562). Every per-element `objectId` obtained via `getProperties` was never released. cdp-use's own `RuntimeClient.getProperties` docstring states: "Object group of the result is inherited from the target object" — since the array itself was created via `Runtime.evaluate` with no `objectGroup`, it (and therefore every property object resolved from it) belongs to no releasable group, so those handles could never be bulk-released and were simply abandoned to leak. This runs on every single `get_dom_tree` call (i.e. every agent step) on any page that has JS click listeners — extremely common, up to 100 elements/step per `_MAX_JS_CLICK_LISTENER_ELEMENTS` — permanently pinning those remote-object handles in the renderer's V8 inspector backend for the life of the CDP session/target. Over a long-running agent session this is an unbounded resource leak in the browser process, directly contradicting the adjacent comment's own stated intent ("Release the array object to avoid memory leaks").
result.self_critique: Before touching code I checked: (1) Is it intentional? The comment right above the release call ("Release the array object to avoid memory leaks") shows leak-avoidance was the explicit goal, so leaving up to 100 per-call element handles unreleased contradicts the code's own stated contract rather than being a deliberate choice. (2) Is it already tested? Grepped tests/ci for `releaseObject`/`objectGroup`/click-listener coverage — none existed; `test_dom_listener_detection.py` and `test_dom_selector_index_collisions.py` cover detection correctness and CDP fanout bounding, not object lifecycle. (3) Does fixing it change public/documented behavior? No — `js_click_listener_backend_ids` (the function's actual output) is untouched; this is purely internal CDP object-lifecycle bookkeeping. (4) Simpler explanation I might be missing? I verified empirically against a real headless Chromium (not just reading the CDP spec): captured the actual per-element `objectId`s `Runtime.getProperties` returns during a real detection pass, then tried releasing one of them a second time myself immediately afterward — on unfixed code the release succeeds (proving the id was still live, i.e. leaked), on fixed code it raises "Could not find object with given id" (proving it was already reclaimed). That closed the loop and confirmed this isn't a misreading of CDP semantics. I also want to flag, for honesty, that I first chased a different bug in the same file: `DomService.detect_pagination_buttons`'s `is_disabled` check compares `attributes.get('disabled')` to the literal string `'true'`, which native `<button disabled>` never produces (its attribute value is `''`). I built a real-browser test for it and it failed — but for the wrong reason: it turned out `detect_pagination_buttons` only ever sees `selector_map`, and disabled elements never reach `selector_map` in the first place (`ClickableElementDetector.is_interactive` excludes any node whose AX tree exposes a truthy `disabled` property, before `detect_pagination_buttons` runs at all). So that string-comparison bug is real but inert/unreachable in the actual pipeline — it doesn't survive scrutiny as something that would "visibly break a real agent session," so I dropped it and picked the click-listener leak instead, which I could prove actually fires in real usage.
result.fix_summary: Added a module-level `_JS_CLICK_LISTENER_OBJECT_GROUP = 'browser_use_click_listener_scan'` constant. Tagged the detection scan's `Runtime.evaluate` call with `'objectGroup': _JS_CLICK_LISTENER_OBJECT_GROUP`, so the returned array and (per CDP's inheritance rule) every element handle later obtained from it via `Runtime.getProperties` belong to one named, bulk-releasable group. Replaced the old single `Runtime.releaseObject(result_object_id)` call with one `Runtime.releaseObjectGroup(objectGroup=_JS_CLICK_LISTENER_OBJECT_GROUP)` call, moved into a `finally` block wrapping Steps 2-3 so cleanup always runs — including when `getProperties` or a `describeNode` batch raises partway through — instead of only on the happy path. This releases the array and every per-element handle it produced in a single round trip, regardless of how many elements were resolved.
